contributions.headingText: Choriocarcinoma is composed of cells of the extraembryonic chorion, including cytotrophoblast, intermediate trophoblast, and syncytiotrophoblast cells.

2C73.Y & XH8PK7 Other specified malignant neoplasms of the ovary & Choriocarcinoma, NOS

2C80.02 & XH8PK7 Germ cell tumour of testis & Choriocarcinoma, NOS

2A00.1Y & XH8PK7 Other specified embryonal tumours of brain & Choriocarcinoma, NOS

Choriocarcinoma occurs in the gonads, mediastinum, and CNS (mostly in the pineal region, followed by the suprasellar compartment, basal ganglia / thalamus, spine, and other locations) {15015791; 30442453; 6006788}.

Choriocarcinoma occurs in 6.4–17.8% of mixed testicular germ cell tumours and is pure in 0.3% {6093440; 15017200; 4148412; 24145647}. It is rare in childhood, except in patients with disorders of sex development {3022907; 6093440}. Detection often follows signs or symptoms attributed to a distant metastasis, such as haemoptysis, an abdominal mass, neurological dysfunction, anaemia, or hypotension. β-hCG is invariably elevated (often > 50 000 IU/L {24145647}), possibly related to gynaecomastia (10%) and thyrotoxicosis (rare). Clinical features of CNS primary pure choriocarcinomas correlate with tumour location, high β-hCG, associated hydrocephalus, and tumoural haemorrhage {15015791; 30442453; 24847965}. Metastatic choriocarcinomas in the brain and spinal cord occur and are frequently associated with tumoural haemorrhage. The symptoms and signs vary from headache to acute change of consciousness. In cases of spinal tumour haemorrhage, patients may present with back pain.

See section Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (male gonadal) . CNS choriocarcinoma occurs in 3.3–5% of all germ cell tumours {9046301; 2991485} and in 5.6% of non-germinomatous tumours {9046301}. It is more frequent in male patients (M:F ratio: 3.4:1). The mean patient age is 13 years (range: 5–22 years), with two peaks in incidence, at 6–11 years and at 13–18 years {30442453}.

See section Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (male gonadal) {16607373; 24249158; 24452629; 24896186; 27391150}. Fewer CNS germ cell tumours exhibit gains of 12p than do testicular and mediastinal examples {12071636; 19801160; 24249158; 24452629}. Gains of CCND2 and PRDM14 (primordial germ cell specification regulator) and losses of RB1 imply involvement of the cyclin/CDK/RB1/E2F pathway {24249158}. Activating mutations involving the MAPK pathway (KIT, RAS family members) and (less frequently) the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway have been identified in germ cell tumours beyond infancy / early childhood {24452629; 24896186; 26956871; 27391150}. More CNS germ cell tumours appear to occur in Down syndrome {28919233} and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) {14670679; 30291793; 31916730} than in the general population.

See section Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (male gonadal) . Clinical and epigenetic studies of germ cell tumours arising after infancy / early childhood {26956871; 27391150; 28078450} suggest a primordial germ cell origin, although alternative origins have also been suggested {17705807; 22926997}.
Choriocarcinoma appears as mostly solid, haemorrhagic and necrotic nodules containing foci (sometimes as a peripheral rim) of solid, greyish-tan tumour.

Choriocarcinoma classically consists of mononucleated trophoblasts (cytotrophoblasts and intermediate trophoblasts) and multinucleated syncytiotrophoblasts, mostly in a haemorrhagic background. Mononucleated trophoblasts (small cytotrophoblasts with some medium-sized and fewer large intermediate trophoblasts) are capped by syncytiotrophoblasts forming plexiform aggregates and protrusions. Cytotrophoblasts have clear to lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, distinct cell boundaries, slightly irregular nuclei, and one or multiple prominent nucleoli displaying frequent mitotic figures. Syncytiotrophoblasts are large, with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm (often containing internalized erythrocytes) and one or multiple nuclei (often dark and smudgy). They may have spindly configurations. Monophasic choriocarcinoma, i.e. sheets of cytotrophoblasts with syncytiotrophoblasts, may occur {9060597}. Vascular invasion is common. β-hCG and hPL are expressed, as well as keratin and sometimes PLAP {18045648; 4038412; 1325276; 25400782}. Syncytiotrophoblasts express inhibin and glypican-3 (GPC3) {9568511; 17122513}, and cytotrophoblasts express SALL4, GDF3, p63, and GATA3 {25188865; 19390421; 19396148; 24145647}.

Diagnosis requires examination of tissue sections and immunohistochemical evaluation, but the presence of syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells in squash or smear preparations raises concern for choriocarcinoma, particularly in a haemorrhagic/necrotic background.

Isochromosome 12p and increased copy numbers of 12p in the majority of choriocarcinomas are helpful diagnostic findings to differentiate from non–germ cell, poorly differentiated malignancies {10357096; 8527395}.
Essential: identification of both syncytiotrophoblastic and cytotrophoblastic elements; β-hCG expression; absence of KIT, D2-40, AFP, and OCT3/4.

See section Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (male gonadal) . In CNS choriocarcinoma, extraneural metastasis is more frequent than leptomeningeal metastasis at diagnosis {2991485; 1501791; 30442453}. Staging without extraneural metastasis follows the Delphi consensus {26370356}.

Choriocarcinoma is highly aggressive, with early haematogenous spread, high stage, and haemorrhagic complications {7141907; 4134907; 1372134; 24145647}. Choriocarcinoma commonly metastasizes to the lungs, liver, gastrointestinal tract, brain, spleen, and adrenals {4148412; 17563738; 24145647}. Elevated serum β-hCG (> 50 000 IU/L) after treatment indicates a poor response {2426944}. Pure/predominant choriocarcinomas have similar outcomes {24145647}. After combination chemotherapy, a 3-year survival rate of 21% is reported {24145647}. Outcome may not be uniformly fatal with standard chemotherapy for metastases confined to the lungs, or after complete resection of residual mass with high-dose chemotherapy and stem cell support {20057969; 17563738; 24145647}.

CNS pure choriocarcinoma (intracranial-predominant) has a median survival time of 22 months, and survival rates of 58.8% and 45.8% at 36 and 60 months, respectively {30442353}. Haematogenous metastases occur in 26.8%, predominantly in the lung {30442453}. Negative prognostic factors are extraneural metastasis {30442453} and a pineal or suprasellar location {15015191; 30442453}; positive indicators include gross total resection {30442453}, postresectional chemotherapy {15015191; 30442453}, and postresectional radiotherapy {15015191}. A high β-hCG level has no prognostic significance {15015191}.
